Work  /  Global Newborn Solutions
Brand identity · Instructional illustration · Print production

Directions that work when you can’t share a language.

DreamWarmer™ keeps newborns warm without electricity, in places where a cold baby is a routine emergency and an incubator is not an option. Two identities, a kit, and a set of instructions with no sentences in them.

Client

Global Newborn Solutions

Role

Brand identity, instructional illustration, pitch deck, packaging application and print production

Years

2019–2020

Product

DreamWarmer™ — non-electric infant warming kit

The whole procedure. Boil, load, pour, wait, slide. The only text in the sequence is 100°C, 30 min and cool 15 min.

The challenge

DreamWarmer is the invention of Anne Hansen, MD, MPH, medical director of the newborn intensive care unit at Boston Children’s Hospital.

A cold newborn is harder to feed, slower to recover and more likely to die, and in a hospital with power the answer to that is an incubator. This device exists because most of the babies at risk are nowhere near one. It runs on wax tubes, boiling water, a thermos and a mat — no electricity, no batteries, nothing to replace — and that simplicity is the whole proposition.

It is also what puts the weight on the instructions. A nurse may meet this device once, mid-shift, with a cold baby already in the room, so whatever she learns has to come off the object itself. The intention was to make the directions visual, so language was never the barrier between her and a warm baby.

The approach

Take the words out, not the detail. Six panels, drawn to one consistent eye level and one line weight. The only text is three numeric callouts and two icons — a thermometer and a stopwatch — both of which a clinician already reads without being taught.

Draw the motion, not the object. Each panel shows the step mid-action: water mid-pour, the lid mid-twist with arrows around it, the mat sliding onto the tubes. A drawing of a sealed thermos tells you nothing. A drawing of a thermos being sealed tells you what to do with your hands.

Put the mark where the user already is. The DreamWarmer logo appears inside the illustrations, on the canister being handled. By the time anyone sees the logo on the box, they have already seen it on the thing in their hands.

Match the object, not the brand guide. The thermos is royal blue, so the sticker is royal blue on white — not the brand orange. The identity exists to be recognized on a shelf in a supply room, which is a job the brand palette would have done worse.

Three use modes, drawn to the same rules: on its own, under a cover, and alongside Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC). The last one matters — the device was designed to complement skin-to-skin care, not replace it, and the drawing had to say so without a caption.

The pitch deck

The company raised philanthropic and NGO funding with a pitch deck. The information came from many places and in many forms. It needed to look and read as one story, built on the brand.

I structured much of the content, wrote and edited parts of it, and came up with how each point would be shown. The type, color and layout rules set for the deck became the visual foundation for Global Newborn Solutions.

The data comes from STEPP testing that Dr. Hansen and her team ran in Rwanda. The job was to make it read at a glance. Newborn deaths became one pie chart. DreamWarmer and two competing warmers sit in one table. The rollout is a map. The product gets one slide.

I wrote the newborn deaths slide. It opens with the scale, 2.7 million babies a year, then asks who is not surviving. The answer is almost all of them are born in low and middle income countries, where an incubator is often not an option. One chart shows the imbalance, 99 percent against 1 percent. That gap is the case for an infant warmer that works without electricity.

Slides from the 2019 pitch deck. Newborn deaths, the device comparison, the product, and the rollout to high-need countries.

Two names, one family

Global Newborn Solutions is the company. DreamWarmer is its product. They needed to read as related without either one disappearing into the other — a company that might make more than one thing, and a product strong enough to be asked for by name.

The company mark is four overlapping circles in four colors, resolving to a white four-petal shape at the center: four parties, one newborn. The product mark narrows that to a single sunrise form inside a leaf, in three of the same four colors. Registered trademark on the company, trademark on the product.

Splitting them was on the table when we first engaged — lead with the product, keep the company behind it. We didn’t. Nobody knew Global Newborn Solutions yet, and going in through the product with no mother ship under it was a risk.

A later site, designed by others, splits them. The split is right for where the company sits now — the trials, the partners and the track record mean DreamWarmer can carry itself. It couldn’t have in 2019.

Delivered as a full package: four colorways each — full color, single-color orange, black and white-reversed — in SVG, PNG and JPG.

Onto the kit

DreamWarmer ships as a kit with a thermos, the wax tubes, the mat and a carry bag. The thermos and the bag carry the mark, both as a circle on royal blue, so the kit reads as one thing in a storeroom full of donated equipment.

The production mechanical for the thermos sticker, with the 4.625″ die keyline. The sticker on the thermos. The kit bag, with the same circle reversed in white.

The site

The 2019 site ran the argument in order: who is not surviving, why cold matters, what the device does, and who stands behind it — Boston Children’s, Harvard, Berkeley Lab, Partners In Health, the Rwandan Ministry of Health.

And one sentence got a band of its own. Anne Hansen is a clinician and she talks like one — thermoregulation, morbidity, neurodevelopment. Somewhere in all of that she said something that was not clinical at all. That is the line that got pulled out, set at display size, and given a dusk sky and her own face above it.

It is still the strongest thing on the page. Looking at it now, the only change I would make is moving it to the top.

Why Cold Matters. The thermometer carries both numbers at once, and the kit is in the hands of someone who uses it rather than sitting on a white background.
The homepage end to end. The quote band sits about two thirds of the way down.
Graphics built for the case, in a deck system rather than the brand system. Navy and a single orange, photography washed back. The identity palette is built to look like a nursery; it is the wrong register for a chart about infant mortality, and a slide behind a speaker needs a ground the brand colors cannot give it.

What the users said

Field interviews with nurses and caregivers were gathered as DreamWarmer went into use. They were collected about the device, not about the drawings — but one of them is the closest thing an instruction set ever gets to a grade.

Nothing made it difficult for me to learn how to use it; it is something that is easy to learn and anyone without experience could learn how to use it.

Nurse

It is true that Kangaroo Mother Care is good because it creates a relationship between mother and baby. To my observation, the infant warmer can increase the baby’s temperature faster — even if the Kangaroo Mother Care is the best.

Nurse

Pad warming takes up a long time before you can save the babies who may abruptly come in for help, and you may find that you have not yet prepared the infant warmer.

Nurse

The third one is the thirty-minute step being a real problem when a cold baby arrives without warning. It is in the record, so it is on this page.

What the design had to do

A device nobody can use doesn’t save anyone, one nobody recognizes doesn’t get reached for, and one nobody funds never gets made at all.

DreamWarmer is hers. Getting it understood, recognized and worth funding was this.

Logos — one for the company, one for the product

Anne Hansen saw the problem in a Rwandan neonatal ward in 2010, and spent the next decade on the answer with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Most clients hand you a product. She handed over a problem she had carried for ten years. Working on it has been an honor.

DreamWarmer is Anne Hansen’s device, and the clinical evidence behind it is hers: Rwanda cluster-randomized trial · Malawi implementation study. Industrial design and manufacturing engineering for the mattress were carried out by a separate firm. The device, the thermos and the instructions have all been redesigned since, and training now runs on video and in person. This page is the 2019–2020 work.
